content: Congenital herpes, also known as birth-acquired herpes, is a herpes virus infection that an infant acquires during or shortly after birth. This condition can present in various ways, ranging from localized skin infections to severe systemic involvement. Symptoms of Congenital Herpes: 1. Localized Skin Infection: Small, fluid-filled blisters (vesicles) may appear on the skin. These blisters can rupture, form crusts, and eventually heal, often leaving mild scarring. 2. Disseminated Herpes: The herpes virus can spread throughout the body, affecting multiple organs. Organs commonly involved include the brain (causing herpes encephalitis), liver, lungs, and kidneys. In some cases, there may be no visible skin blisters despite systemic involvement. 3. Severe Symptoms in Newborns with Disseminated Herpes: Easy bleeding. Breathing difficulties, including rapid breathing (tachypnea), grunting, flaring nostrils, or periods of apnea (temporary cessation of breathing). Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin due to lack of oxygen). Lethargy, poor feeding, and low body temperature (hypothermia). Neonatal jaundice. Seizures, coma, or shock. Skin lesions, such as fluid-filled blisters. 4. Intrauterine Herpes (rare): Can result in severe complications, including: Eye diseases, such as chorioretinitis (inflammation of the retina). Severe brain damage. Skin sores (lesions). Causes of Congenital Herpes: 1. Modes of Transmission: Infection can occur in the uterus (intrauterine herpes), though this is rare. The most common mode of transmission is during delivery, as the baby passes through the birth canal of a mother with active genital herpes. Postpartum transmission can occur through close contact, such as kissing or touching by someone with active herpes sores. 2. Maternal Factors: Mothers with active genital herpes at the time of delivery are at higher risk of transmitting the virus to their baby. Some mothers may have internal herpes sores (inside the vagina) and be unaware of their infection. Individuals with a history of herpes infections, even if asymptomatic, can unknowingly transmit the virus. 3. Types of Herpes Virus: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2, genital herpes) is the most common cause of neonatal herpes. Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1, oral herpes) can also cause infection in newborns. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: If a newborn exhibits any symptoms of birth-acquired herpes, including skin lesions, immediate medical evaluation is essential. Diagnostic Tests: 1. Specific Tests for Herpes: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test from vesicle scrapings. Vesicle culture. Spinal fluid culture. MRI of the head. Electroencephalogram (EEG). 2. Additional Tests for Severely Ill Infants: Blood gas analysis. Coagulation studies (PT, PTT). Complete blood count (CBC). Liver function tests. Treatment Options: 1. Antiviral Therapy: Intravenous administration of antiviral medications, typically acyclovir, is the standard treatment. Treatment duration may extend for several weeks. 2. Supportive Care: Management of complications such as seizures or shock. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission is often required for critically ill infants. Prognosis: 1. Systemic Herpes or Encephalitis: Despite early treatment with antiviral medications, the prognosis is often poor. 2. Localized Skin Disease: Vesicles may recur even after treatment, increasing the risk of long-term complications such as learning disabilities. Possible Complications: Secondary bacterial or fungal infections of skin lesions. Coma or death. Developmental delays. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) leading to excessive bleeding. Eye problems, including chorioretinitis or keratitis. Gastrointestinal issues, such as diarrhea. Hepatitis, jaundice, or liver failure. Respiratory complications, including pneumonia or pneumonitis. Neurological issues, including seizures or brain damage. Shock and respiratory distress. Prevention: 1. Maternal Precautions: Pregnant women should inform their healthcare provider if they have a history of genital herpes. Safer sexual practices can reduce the risk of acquiring genital herpes during pregnancy. 2. Postnatal Precautions: Individuals with active cold sores (herpes labialis) should avoid contact with newborns. Caregivers with cold sores should wear surgical masks and practice strict hand hygiene before handling the infant. 3. Medical Guidance: Mothers should consult their healthcare provider to discuss strategies for minimizing the risk of herpes transmission to their baby.
